title: AI Hell Freezes Over — Mystery AI Hype Theater 3000 Ep. 23 (year-end AI Hell round-up, with the Cohen/Bard filing and the E&W judicial AI guidance)
pub: Mystery AI Hype Theater 3000 (DAIR Institute) — Ep. 23, recorded live 22 December 2023, podcast edition published 10 January 2024
author: Emily M. Bender · Alex Hanna

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Human oversight: Accountability is not effective control
st.an: The source criticises Tesla’s autonomy advertising and hype, but does not substantively address whether human oversight provides effective control, requires independent verification, protects expertise development, or is adequately governed by professional rules. Its discussion is therefore adjacent to, rather than a position on, the cluster’s proposition.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s core proposition that legal AI can deliver rapid gains on bounded work while creating serious verification and competence risks. Its sanctions example shows that nominal human review did not prevent fabricated citations from reaching court, and its warning about e-discovery reinforces that risks extend beyond court drafting. It does not establish broader productivity, labour-market or organisational effects.
qs: Within seconds, the artificial intelligence chatbot had completed the document.
While surveying the brief he realized to his horror that the AI chatbot had made up several fake lawsuit citations.

st.t: Task substitution: Complementarity can still reshape staffing
st.an: Bender supports the cluster’s bounded account of task substitution: AI can produce legal drafts rapidly, but fabricated citations make effective human verification and professional accountability indispensable. The source illustrates consequential failure rather than establishing model error rates or broader staffing effects.
qs: Within seconds, the artificial intelligence chatbot had completed the document.
While surveying the brief he realized to his horror that the AI chatbot had made up several fake lawsuit citations.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source aligns with the synthesis that fluent, high-quality task output does not establish general competence and that consequential legal uses require verification and human accountability. Its legal examples illustrate unsafe reliance and risks even in routine workflows, though it does not materially develop the synthesis’s operating-model redesign analysis.
qs: "Proposes and tests the hypothesis that models acquire generative capabilities that exceed their ability to understand the outputs."  Which you know my reaction to that is just like duh, like this is--what do you mean--yes they can spit stuff out but they do not understand.

kp.k: Judicial guidance opens court work to generative AI
kp.d: Reading Thomas Germain's Gizmodo report, Hanna describes Judicial Office guidance permitting ChatGPT and other AI tools for writing rulings and other tasks. Although the report uses UK-wide language, the quoted institutional remit concerns England and Wales. Hanna criticises allowing adoption despite previous failures. This is commentary on reporting about guidance, not an analysis of the guidance's full permissions or safeguards.
qs: The UK Judicial Office issued guidance Tuesday permitting judges to use ChatGPT and other AI tools to write legal rulings and perform several other tasks.
The guidance is the first step in a proposed suite of future work to support report the judiciary and their interactions with AI.
Uh so they're just allowing some usage of this to seep into this legal domain, even though so much of this has gone wrong.

kp.k: Cohen filing illustrates fabricated authorities and verification burdens
kp.d: Bender reads a Southern District of New York filing concerning David M. Schwartz's 29 November 2023 motion for early termination of Michael Cohen's supervised release. The court could not locate cited cases, and replacement counsel reported being unable to verify them. Bender speculates that generative AI, possibly ChatGPT, produced the earlier filing; the spoken transcript does not establish Bard's involvement despite the supplied document heading. Hanna stresses the wasted work imposed on court clerks.
qs: On November 29th, 2023, David M. Schwartz, counsel of record for Defendant Michael Cohen, filed a motion for early termination of supervised release.

While several cases were cited in the initial motion filed by different counsel, undersigned counsel was not engaged at the time and must inform the court that it has been unable to verify those citations.
I feel really bad for the the clerks at this court. They're just trying to do--they're wasting all this time trying to find these fake court cases

kp.k: Junior lawyer's time savings culminate in professional consequences
kp.d: Quoting a Washington Post article published 16 November 2023, Bender recounts Zachariah Crabill's use of ChatGPT to complete a motion during a heavy workload that May, two years after law school. He sent it to his boss for review and filed it in Colorado before discovering fabricated citations. The account reports an apology, referral to the statewide attorney-complaints office and dismissal from his job. Bender treats detection as the legal system functioning; the episode does not establish whether the boss actually reviewed the motion.
qs: Zachariah Crabill was two years out of law school, burned out and nervous, when his bosses added another case to his workload this May.
Crabill sent it to his boss for review and filed it in the Colorado court.
While surveying the brief he realized to his horror that the AI chatbot had made up several fake lawsuit citations.
The judge reported him to a statewide office that handles attorney complaints.
And he was fired.

kp.k: Inevitability rhetoric sustains adoption after demonstrated failures
kp.d: The Washington Post account quotes Crabill continuing to believe AI is law's future after his filing incident. Having started his own company, he reportedly intended to use lawyer-specific AI tools for writing and research rather than ChatGPT, motivated by avoiding being left behind. The hosts criticise this response. Hanna's suggestion that venture capitalists would probably reward him is speculation, not evidence of financing or of specialised tools' reliability.
qs: Now he has his own company and says he's likely to use AI tools designed specifically for lawyers to aid in his writing and his research, instead of ChatGPT.
He says he doesn't want to be left behind.
'There's no point in being a naysayer,' Crabill said, 'or being against something that is invariably going to become the way of the future.'

kp.k: E-discovery automation can create document-production risks
kp.d: Bender quotes Brown professor Suresh Venkatasubramanian warning that even apparently routine legal work such as e-discovery carries risks if ChatGPT causes subpoenaed documents to be omitted. This is a hypothetical warning, expressly qualified by his statement that he is not a lawyer, rather than a documented discovery failure.
qs: But even using AI for legal grunt work such as e-discovery comes with risks, says Venkatasubramanian, the Brown professor.
If they've been subpoenaed and they produced some documents and not others because of a ChatGPT error -- I'm not a lawyer but that could be a problem.

kp.k: Undisclosed AI legislative drafting raises public-accountability concerns
kp.d: Hanna reads AP reporting that Porto Alegre passed an ordinance in October which councilman Ramiro Rosário later disclosed had been written by ChatGPT. The proposal concerned replacement charges for stolen water meters; Rosário reportedly presented it unchanged to 35 fellow councillors without disclosure. He defended secrecy as necessary for approval. The hosts reject that defence and argue elected officials should write and ensure the effectiveness of legislation themselves.
qs: He then presented it to his 35 peers on the council without making a single change or even letting them know about its unprecedented origin.
If I had revealed it before, the proposal certainly wouldn't even have been taken to a vote.
It's like no, it's unfair to the population to not do the job that you were elected to do.
If it's a good idea, you can write the stuff yourself and make sure you're writing legislation that actually works.

kp.k: Financial-document testing questions production-ready language-model reliability
kp.d: Hanna recounts CNBC reporting on Patronus AI research finding frequent failures on questions derived from SEC filings. The transcript mentions 79 percent correct answers on Patronus's new test without clearly identifying the corresponding model, sample size or test conditions. Patronus co-founder Anand Kannappan calls performance inadequate for automated production use. The hosts extend this into a broader objection to relying on generated text where answer validity matters.
qs: Large language models similar to the one at the heart of ChatGPT frequently fail to answer questions derived from Securities and Exchange Commission filings, new research finds.
79 percent of answers right on Patronus's new AI test
It has to be much higher for it to really work in an automated and production-ready way.
So at any point where you actually care about the validity of the answer, don't use the synthetic media math-sticated data extruding machine.

kp.k: Fluent generation does not establish understanding or human reasoning
kp.d: The hosts discuss research proposing that generative capabilities can exceed demonstrated understanding, endorsing its caution against human-intelligence analogies while arguing the result should not be surprising. They also challenge psychological interpretations of language-model performance on cognitive reflection and semantic-illusion tasks. Bender demands construct validity before psychological methods are applied to these systems; Hanna rejects reporting that emotional prompting signals progress toward AGI.
qs: Proposes and tests the hypothesis that models acquire generative capabilities that exceed their ability to understand the outputs.
Generative AI in language and vision can produce high quality generations. Paradoxically, however, models have trouble demonstrating selective or interrogative understanding of these modalities.
psychological methodologies need to be validated for construct validity for these things before you use them
the claim, the jump that it's better that's you're getting closer to AGI--I'm just like what in the what in the heck.

kp.k: Training-data disclosure demystifies apparent model capabilities
kp.d: The hosts discuss an appendix disclosing chess games in GPT-4's pretraining dataset and quote commentators linking apparent chess competence to that training exposure. They favour disclosure as a way to explain model behaviour rather than treating capabilities as mysterious. Bender's broader claim that capabilities probably reflect training data, or merely appear to exist, is her interpretation rather than a reported experimental result.
qs: The GPT-4 pretraining dataset included chess games in the format of move sequence known as Portable Game Notation (PGN).
It's almost like releasing information on the training set helps explain the capabilities of these models. We should do this more.
So yeah, basically if it can do it it's probably because it's in the training data. Um or it only looks like it can do it.

kp.k: Data-sharing arrangements weaken individual control and consent
kp.d: Bender describes CNBC reporting that Dropbox users must opt out of sharing with OpenAI and that files shared with another Dropbox AI user could still be transmitted. Separately, she reports that Underline solicited opt-in permission to use conference presentation samples for model training while promising anonymity. She challenges that promise because the material is video and says collective objections led Underline to abandon sharing with an unidentified third party, while noting a follow-up had not yet been sent.
qs: even if you've opted out any files shared with another person who is using Dropbox AI could still be sent to open AI servers.
Please click to indicate your acceptance.
This is completely anonymous, with no identification of you or your talk to any outside party ever.
It's video. That is like inherently non anonymous.

kp.k: Healthcare adoption exposes testing gaps and discriminatory risks
kp.d: The hosts contrast Deloitte survey beliefs about healthcare benefits with Politico reporting of AI diagnosing conditions and recommending treatment without consistent medical-device-style regulation. They quote Venkatasubramanian's concern about inadequate testing in patient-facing uses and reporting of New York City's effort against racially biased clinical algorithms. These are reported concerns and survey perceptions, not demonstrated benefits or a systematic evaluation by the hosts.
qs: Another 46% said it it could make healthcare more affordable.
AI is diagnosing diseases and recommending treatments, but the systems aren't always regulated like drugs or medical devices.
There's no good testing going on, and then they're being used in patient facing situations and that's really bad.
New York City has formed a coalition to end racism in clinical algorithms

kp.k: Insurer incentives may favour harmful automated decisions
kp.d: Bender cites Beth Mole's 16 November Ars Technica reporting on a lawsuit alleging UnitedHealth used an AI model with a 90% error rate to deny care. She connects this allegation to the hosts' earlier prediction that insurers would use model outputs as excuses for denial. The percentage is a lawsuit allegation relayed through journalism, not an independently established error rate in this transcript.
qs: UnitedHealth uses AI model with 90% error rate to deny care, lawsuit alleges.
For the largest health insurer in the US, AI's error rate is like a feature, not a bug.
the health insurance companies were going to be chomping at the bit to um basically take the output of these systems as an excuse to deny care.

kp.k: Autonomy claims conceal continuing human operational work
kp.d: Reading CNBC coverage, Hanna reports Cruise robotaxis needed human assistance every four to five miles, with roughly one remote assistant per 15 to 20 driverless vehicles before operations were grounded. The company distinguished wayfinding assistance from remote driving; its CEO said assistance occupied 2–4% of time in complex urban settings and further optimisation offered little cost benefit. Bender interprets this as an economic barrier to the autonomy being sold; her claim of underpayment is commentary, not wage evidence supplied here.
qs: Cruise confirms robotaxis rely on human assistance every four to five miles.
Human advisors generally provide quote 'wayfinding intel' to the robotaxis, and do not drive them remotely, company spokesman said.
Cruise AVs are being remotely assisted 2-4% of the time on average in complex urban environments.
This is low enough already that there isn't a huge cost benefit to optimizing much further, especially given how useful it is to have humans review things in certain situations.

kp.k: AI production relies on vulnerable data-labelling workers
kp.d: The hosts cite Wired reporting that data-labelling providers inadvertently hire young teenagers, sometimes exposing them to traumatic content, and that a company in high-wage Finland uses prisoners for AI training work. Bender interprets the Finnish case as seeking a cheap labour source where Finnish-language workers would otherwise be difficult to recruit at low pay. These examples concern production labour behind AI, not documented displacement of legal professionals.
qs: Companies that provide big tech with I--AI data labeling services are inadvertently hiring young teens to work their platforms, often exposing them to traumatic content.
In high-wage Finland, where where clickworkers are rare, one company has discovered a novel labor force--prisoners.

kp.k: Synthetic journalism threatens provenance and public trust
kp.d: The hosts criticise OpenAI's Axel Springer agreement, arguing that access to vetted journalism does not make generated output journalism. They also cite reporting that Adobe Stock sold generated Israel–Hamas conflict images, some republished without AI labels, and that Sports Illustrated used apparently fictitious authors with generated headshots. Their emphasis is on provenance, disclosure and replacing accountable reporting; the transcript does not establish that all the Sports Illustrated article text was generated.
qs: papier-mâché made of good journalism is not good journalism, it's still synthetic text that's been extruded and maths-sticated.
Futurism notes that a handful of small publications have ran these images without labeling them as AI
Sports Illustrated appears to have published affiliate articles under the bylines of fake writers, complete with made up bios and AI generated headshots.

kp.k: Life-event research must be distinguished from individual prediction
kp.d: The hosts discuss life2vec research using Danish registry histories covering health, education, occupation, income, address and working hours at day-to-day resolution. The paper claims predictive performance advantages for outcomes including early mortality and personality; no quantitative advantage is supplied. They quote contributor Anna Rogers rejecting USA Today's 'doom calculator' framing and any decision-making use, especially outside the specific Danish sample. Bender distinguishes potentially useful population-level policy analysis from predicting individuals' futures and acknowledges the paper's data safeguards.
qs: Our models allow us to predict diverse outcomes ranging from early mortality to per--personality nuances
The paper uses prediction of registry life events to learn representations that could be used for social science research.
It is not meant as any kind of 'doom calculator,' especially outside of a very specific Danish sample and especially for any kind of decision making.
it shouldn't be framed as we're going to predict what's coming in this person's life next.

kp.k: AI inevitability narratives obscure human purposes and relationships
kp.d: The episode closes by endorsing Angie Wong's New Yorker illustrated essay, which questions equating human worth with efficient output or machine performance. Bender highlights its distinction between a child's lived experience and an LLM's language production, and its grounding of meaning in human connection. This is an explicitly normative framework rather than empirical evidence about professional competence or labour-market outcomes.
qs: They are the least useful, the least creative and the least likely to pass a bar exam.
A toddler has a life, and learns language to describe it. An LLM learns language but has no life of its own to describe.
But she goes through this and basically finds meaning in connection

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The episode presents generative AI as entering judicial drafting, legal research and legislative drafting while introducing fabricated authorities, additional checking work and professional risks.
pts.d: Bender and Hanna argue that adoption is proceeding despite failures. The judicial-use claim comes from Thomas Germain's Gizmodo reporting, quoted in the episode, about Judicial Office guidance for England and Wales; it is not an independently established finding by the hosts. In the Cohen matter, Bender describes apparently nonexistent citations and tentatively attributes the earlier filing to generative AI, saying 'maybe ChatGPT'; the transcript does not establish Bard's involvement despite the document heading. Hanna explicitly identifies the resulting burden on court clerks. The hosts also discuss Washington Post reporting about Zachariah Crabill's AI-generated citations and dismissal. Crabill's belief that AI is the future of law is a quoted third-party prediction, not the hosts' position. Likewise, Suresh Venkatasubramanian's warning about omitted subpoenaed documents is a quoted, conditional concern rather than an observed e-discovery failure. On legislation, Hanna criticises undisclosed chatbot drafting in Porto Alegre, while Bender argues elected officials should write legislation and ensure it works. Hanna's suggestion that investors may reward Crabill is speculation, not evidence of financing.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The legal discussion relies on a court filing, reported incidents and reporting about official guidance, not systematic performance or market data.
pts.d: Bender reads from a Southern District of New York filing concerning Michael Cohen, including the court's inability to locate cited cases and replacement counsel's inability to verify them. This supports an incident-specific claim about fabricated or unverifiable authorities; it does not measure a model's hallucination rate. Washington Post reporting supplies the Crabill example, including a brief with fabricated citations, a judicial referral and reported dismissal. The episode does not establish a specific fine against Crabill, notwithstanding the quoted article headline. AP reporting supplies the Porto Alegre example: a councillor reportedly submitted an unchanged ChatGPT proposal without disclosing its origin, and the council enacted it. Gizmodo reporting supplies the account of judicial guidance, but the transcript does not reproduce its complete safeguards or permitted-use conditions. There are no legal benchmarks, adoption surveys, quantified productivity studies or forecasts of legal-market size.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The claims concern events reported during 2023 and immediate reliance risks, rather than a dated forecast of profession-wide transformation.
pts.d: The episode was recorded on 22 December 2023. The Cohen motion is dated 29 November 2023. The Crabill article was published on 16 November 2023 and describes work undertaken in May. The Porto Alegre ordinance reportedly passed in October. The judicial guidance is described through contemporary reporting as issued on a Tuesday, without an exact date in the quoted discussion. The principal risk condition is reliance on generated material that has not been successfully verified before filing or use. The e-discovery warning is explicitly hypothetical and qualified by its speaker's acknowledgement that he is not a lawyer. Crabill's prediction of inevitable adoption has no deadline and refers to his intended use of legal-specific AI rather than general ChatGPT; the episode supplies no evidence that switching tools resolves the problem. Hanna's forecast of possible investor rewards is similarly undated and speculative.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The affected groups are practising lawyers, clients, court staff, judges, legislators and the public, with impacts framed around professional accountability, checking burdens and undisclosed use.
pts.d: For lawyers, the Crabill account contrasts an initially perceived drafting-time saving with fabricated citations, a disciplinary referral and dismissal. For court clerks and successor counsel, the Cohen episode entails searching for and attempting to verify nonexistent authorities. Clients are implicated through the reliability of their representation, although the episode does not quantify client losses or establish an adverse outcome caused by the citations. Judges and tribunal members in England and Wales are the users covered by the discussed guidance, and litigants are potentially affected by AI-assisted judicial work. In Porto Alegre, fellow councillors were reportedly not informed of the proposal's origin; residents and taxpayers were affected by the resulting ordinance. The source does not make a supported claim about law-firm staffing structures, associate displacement, billing models or competition between law firms and alternative legal service providers.
